items.title: Working from Home
items.text:
When Hoa's company let staff work from home two days a week, she was delighted. She would save an hour of travel every day and could finally have breakfast with her children.
The first month was not as easy as she had expected. Her flat was small, so she had to work at the kitchen table. Her neighbours were building a new bathroom, and the noise made phone meetings difficult. She also noticed that she was working longer hours, because there was no clear moment when the day ended.
So Hoa made some changes. She bought a small desk and put it in the corner of the bedroom. She started every home day by getting dressed as if she were going to the office, and she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly. On Fridays she went to a café near her flat for two hours, just to see other people.
Now, she says, home days are her most productive. "The secret," she explains, "is to treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home."

qs.q: Why was the first month difficult for Hoa?
qs.a: Her flat was small and noisy, and she worked too long
w: Her children were at home all day
Her company asked her to come back
qs.why: “Her flat was small… the noise made phone meetings difficult… she was working longer hours.”

qs.q: What does Hoa do at six o'clock?
qs.a: She switches off her computer
qs.why: “she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly.”

qs.q: What is Hoa's advice?
qs.a: Keep work and home life separate
w: Work in a café every day
Don't work from home at all
qs.why: “treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home.”

items.title: A Message from the Sports Centre
items.tvi: Thông báo của trung tâm thể thao
items.text:
Dear members,
From Monday 3 June, the swimming pool will be closed for four weeks while we replace the old changing rooms. We know many of you swim every morning, so we have made an agreement with Riverside Hotel, which is only ten minutes' walk from here. Members can use the hotel pool free of charge between 6 and 9 a.m. Please show your membership card at the hotel reception.
All other activities, including yoga, the gym and tennis, will continue as normal. However, the car park will be smaller during the building work, so we suggest you come by bike or bus if possible.
To say sorry for the trouble, every member will receive one extra month of membership at no cost. You do not need to do anything; it will be added to your account automatically.
If you have any questions, please speak to Mai at the front desk or email info@greenpark.vn.
Thank you for your patience.
Green Park Sports Centre

qs.q: Why is the pool closing?
qs.a: The changing rooms are being rebuilt
qs.why: “closed for four weeks while we replace the old changing rooms.”

qs.q: What must members do to swim at the hotel?
qs.a: Show their membership card
qs.why: “Please show your membership card at the hotel reception.”

qs.q: How will members get their extra month?
qs.a: It will be added automatically
w: They must ask Mai at the desk
qs.why: “it will be added to your account automatically.”

items.title: The Boy Who Fixed Bicycles
items.text:
When Tuan was twelve, his bicycle broke on the way to school. His family had no money for a new one, so he took it apart in the yard and tried to repair it himself. It took him three weekends, and he made many mistakes, but in the end it worked.
Soon his neighbours began bringing him their broken bikes. At first he did it for free, but his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging a small amount and saved every coin in a tin box.
By the time he was sixteen, Tuan had saved enough to rent a tiny space at the market. He painted a sign that said 'Tuan's Bikes' and worked there every afternoon after school. His teachers were worried that he would fall behind, but his marks actually improved, because he had learned to plan his time carefully.
Today Tuan is twenty-five and owns two shops. He still keeps the old tin box on his desk. "It reminds me," he says, "that every big thing starts with something small."

qs.q: Why did Tuan repair his own bicycle?
qs.a: His family couldn't afford a new one
w: He wanted to start a business
qs.why: “His family had no money for a new one.”

qs.q: What did his grandmother teach him?
qs.a: That he should be paid for his work
qs.why: “his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging…”

qs.q: What happened to his school marks?
qs.a: They got better
qs.why: “his marks actually improved.”

items.title: Should Students Wear Uniforms?
items.tvi: Học sinh có nên mặc đồng phục?
items.text:
Last week our school asked students what they thought about uniforms. Here are two opinions.
Linh, 15: "I'm in favour of uniforms. In the morning I don't have to think about what to wear, so I save time. Also, nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure. Some people say uniforms are boring, but we can still show our personality with our bags, hair and shoes."
Khang, 16: "I disagree. Uniforms are expensive, because we have to buy them from the school shop and they don't last long. They are also uncomfortable in hot weather. I think we should be allowed to wear our own clothes, with a few simple rules, for example no very short skirts or offensive slogans. Learning how to dress well is part of growing up."
The head teacher says the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.

qs.q: According to Linh, why do uniforms reduce pressure?
qs.a: Students can't see who is rich or poor
w: Students don't need to buy bags
qs.why: “nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure.”

qs.q: What does Khang say about the price of uniforms?
qs.a: They cost a lot and wear out quickly
w: They are cheaper than normal clothes
qs.why: “Uniforms are expensive… they don't last long.”

qs.q: What will happen next?
qs.a: The school will decide after talking to parents
qs.why: “the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.”

items.title: My First Job Interview
items.tvi: Buổi phỏng vấn xin việc đầu tiên
items.text:
I had my first job interview last Tuesday, for a part-time position at a bookshop. I was so nervous that I couldn't eat breakfast. I arrived twenty minutes early, which was a good idea, because I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.
The manager, Mrs Ha, was friendly. She asked me why I wanted the job and what books I liked. I had prepared answers to these questions, so I felt more relaxed. Then she asked me something I hadn't expected: "Tell me about a time when you made a mistake." My mind went blank for a few seconds. Then I told her about a group project at school where I forgot to send an important file, and explained how I now write everything in a planner.
At the end, she showed me around the shop and introduced me to two of the staff. Yesterday she phoned to offer me the job. She said that my answer about the mistake was the reason she chose me, because it showed I could learn from problems.

qs.q: Why was it good that the writer arrived early?
qs.a: The writer got lost before finding the shop
qs.why: “I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.”

qs.q: Which question surprised the writer?
qs.a: A question about a mistake they had made
qs.why: “she asked me something I hadn't expected: Tell me about a time when you made a mistake.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Ha choose the writer?
qs.a: The writer showed they could learn from problems
w: The writer knew a lot about books
The writer was the first to arrive
qs.why: “it showed I could learn from problems.”

items.title: Plastic in the Sea
items.text:
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the oceans. Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea. Once it is in the water, plastic does not disappear. Sunlight and waves break it into very small pieces, called microplastics, which fish and birds eat by mistake.
Scientists have found microplastics in salt, in tap water and even in the air. They are still studying what this means for human health, but many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.
There are some simple things everyone can do. Carrying a reusable bottle and bag is a good start. Saying no to plastic straws and choosing products with less packaging also helps. In some cities, shops give a small discount to customers who bring their own containers.
Governments have a role too. Several countries have banned single-use plastic bags, and a few have introduced deposit schemes, where people get money back when they return bottles. In places where these schemes exist, far fewer bottles are found on beaches.

qs.q: How does much of the plastic reach the sea?
qs.a: Rivers carry it from cities
w: Ships throw it into the water
qs.why: “Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea.”

qs.q: What do experts think we should do about health risks?
qs.a: Act now without waiting for results
w: Wait until the studies are finished
qs.why: “many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.”

qs.q: What happens where deposit schemes exist?
qs.a: There are fewer bottles on beaches
qs.why: “far fewer bottles are found on beaches.”

items.title: The Night Market Cook
items.tvi: Người nấu ăn ở chợ đêm
items.text:
Mrs Lan has sold noodle soup at the same night market for thirty years. She starts preparing at two in the afternoon, cooking the broth slowly with beef bones, onions and spices. By six o'clock, when the market opens, there is already a queue at her stall.
Many customers are regulars who have been eating there since they were children. Others are tourists who have read about her online. A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors from Korea, Australia and France have come to try it. Mrs Lan does not speak much English, but she has learned to say "spicy?" and "one more?" with a big smile.
Last year a restaurant group offered her a job as head cook in their new restaurant in the city centre. The salary was good and she would work in a modern kitchen. She refused. "At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces when they taste the soup," she says. "In a big kitchen I would just be a name on a menu."
Her daughter now helps her at weekends and is slowly learning the recipe, which has never been written down.

qs.q: Why do many tourists visit Mrs Lan's stall?
qs.a: A blogger wrote about her soup
w: Her stall is in a hotel
qs.why: “A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors… have come.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Lan refuse the restaurant job?
qs.a: She wanted to keep contact with her customers
qs.why: “At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces.”

qs.q: What do we learn about the recipe?
qs.a: It exists only in Mrs Lan's memory
w: It is printed on the menu
qs.why: “the recipe, which has never been written down.”

items.title: Volunteers Wanted
items.text:
Are you free on Saturday mornings? Do you enjoy working with children? Sunflower Library is looking for volunteers to help with our weekend reading club.
The club is for children aged six to ten who find reading difficult. Volunteers read stories with small groups, play word games and help the children choose books to borrow. You don't need to be a teacher, but you should be patient, friendly and able to read clearly. All volunteers receive a two-hour training session before they start.
We ask volunteers to come at least twice a month for six months, because the children feel more confident when they see the same faces. Sessions run from 8.30 to 11.00, and we provide free drinks and snacks.
Last year, eighty percent of the children in the club improved their reading level by at least one grade. Many parents told us their children now read at home for fun.
To apply, fill in the form on our website before 15 August. We will invite you for a short chat, and training begins on 1 September.

qs.q: Who is the reading club for?
qs.a: Children who have problems with reading
w: Children who want to become teachers
Adults who want to learn English
qs.why: “The club is for children aged six to ten who find reading difficult.”

qs.q: Why must volunteers come regularly?
qs.a: Children feel more confident with familiar faces
w: Volunteers are paid by the month
qs.why: “the children feel more confident when they see the same faces.”

qs.q: What happens after you send the form?
qs.a: You are invited for a short conversation
w: You start working the next Saturday
You must take a reading test
qs.why: “We will invite you for a short chat.”

items.title: Learning to Drive at Forty
items.tvi: Học lái xe ở tuổi bốn mươi
items.text:
For most of my life I relied on buses, taxis and my husband to get around. I always told myself I was too nervous to drive. But when we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day, I realised I had no choice.
My first lesson was terrible. I stopped the engine five times and drove round a roundabout twice because I was too scared to leave it. My instructor, a calm man called Duc, simply laughed and said, "Everyone does that."
What helped me most was practising in a quiet car park on Sunday mornings with my son, who had passed his test the year before. He was surprisingly patient, which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.
I failed my first driving test because I forgot to check my mirror before turning. I was disappointed, but I booked another test immediately. Six weeks later I passed. Now I drive to work every day, and last month I drove my mother to the coast for her birthday. The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.

qs.q: Why did the writer decide to learn to drive?
qs.a: Public transport in her new town was very limited
w: Her son needed a lift to school
qs.why: “we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day.”

qs.q: Why does the writer find her son's patience funny?
qs.a: She had once taught him to ride a bike
qs.why: “which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.”

qs.q: How does the writer feel now?
qs.a: She enjoys her independence but regrets starting late
w: She is still afraid of driving
qs.why: “The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.”

items.title: Review: The Lighthouse Café
items.tvi: Nhận xét: quán cà phê Ngọn Hải Đăng
items.text:
The Lighthouse Café opened in March in an old fishing house next to the harbour. The owners have kept the original wooden walls and decorated them with old maps and photos of local fishermen, which gives the place a warm, relaxed feeling.
I visited on a Wednesday afternoon. The menu is short but interesting, with local seafood, salads and homemade cakes. I had the grilled fish with lemon rice, which was fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price. My friend's coconut cake, on the other hand, was huge and delicious.
Service was friendly but slow. We waited almost twenty minutes for our drinks, and the waiter apologised, explaining that two staff members were ill. Still, I would recommend booking a table at weekends, because the terrace with its sea view fills up quickly.
Overall, the Lighthouse Café is a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal. Go for the view and the cakes, and don't be in a hurry.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the grilled fish?
qs.a: It was good but too small for the price
w: It was the biggest dish on the menu
qs.why: “fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price.”

qs.q: Why was the service slow that day?
qs.a: Two staff members were ill
qs.why: “two staff members were ill.”

qs.q: Who would enjoy this café most?
qs.a: People who want a long, relaxed meal
w: People who need a quick lunch
People who want a large menu
qs.why: “a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal.”
